questions.q: What is the main skill emphasis of the NFT marketplace capstone, compared to Project 1's DeFi protocol?
options: Pool accounting and AMM math
Marketplace/escrow logic plus a real indexing problem that a raw node RPC can't solve
Consensus algorithm design
Mobile app development
questions.explain: Project 1 emphasized DeFi pool mechanics; Project 2 emphasizes marketplace/escrow logic and indexing, since questions like 'show all active listings' can't be answered efficiently by a node's raw RPC interface.

questions.q: In this capstone's scope, how does a listed NFT stay with its owner?
options: It doesn't -- it's always transferred into the marketplace contract immediately
The owner mails a signed paper deed to the marketplace
The seller only grants the marketplace an approval; the NFT itself stays in the seller's wallet until it sells
The NFT is burned and re-minted after sale
questions.explain: This project uses an approval-based pattern: the seller approves the marketplace contract to transfer the NFT later, but keeps holding it until a sale actually completes.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly out of scope for this capstone's marketplace contract?
options: Royalty payout via ERC-2981
Fixed-price listings in ETH
English/Dutch auctions and ERC-20 payment
The cancel-listing flow
questions.explain: Auctions, bundled/ERC-1155 batch listings, lazy minting, and ERC-20 payment are all called out as out of scope, to keep the project small enough to fully finish.

questions.q: Why does the contract's buy flow pay the royalty and transfer the NFT in a single transaction?
options: So gas fees are lower overall
So there's no intermediate state where payment happened but the NFT transfer didn't, or vice versa
Because Solidity requires all function calls to be atomic by default, so this is unavoidable
Because two separate transactions aren't technically possible on Ethereum
questions.explain: Bundling payment, royalty payout, and transfer into one transaction guarantees atomicity -- either everything succeeds together, or the whole transaction reverts and nothing happens.

questions.q: Why can't 'show me every currently active listing' be answered directly by calling the marketplace contract's own functions on a node?
options: A node's RPC interface doesn't support arbitrary aggregate queries like that; you need an indexer that processes the contract's events into queryable data
The contract deletes all data immediately after each listing
Ethereum nodes don't support read calls of any kind
It actually can be answered directly, with no indexer needed
questions.explain: This is the same indexing problem covered in the Blockchain APIs & Backend course: a node exposes narrow read calls, not arbitrary queries, so an indexer (subgraph or custom listener) is needed to answer questions like 'all active listings.'
